# Inference-Compute Budget vs. Attack Step Completion: Replication Across Model Families

**Problem:** The AISI 2026 finding that performance scales log-linearly with inference-time compute (10M→100M tokens yields up to 59% gains) has only been documented on a narrow set of frontier models. It is unknown whether this scaling law holds for open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen families).

**Direction:** Replicate the AISI inference-token budget experiment using open-weight models on a simplified 5-10 step cyber range (e.g., a local CTF-style Metasploitable VM chain). Vary token budget from 1K to 500K across model families and plot steps completed vs. log(tokens). Test whether log-linear scaling is a universal phenomenon or specific to frontier closed models.

**Why it matters:** If log-linear scaling is universal, even cheap open-weight models become significantly more dangerous with increased inference budget. If it is not, this tells evaluators which model families pose greater scaling risk. Directly addresses the lack of longitudinal cross-model comparison methodology.

**Relevant context:** Folkerts et al. 2026 (AISI) found log-linear scaling with no plateau: steps completed rose from 1.7 (GPT-4o) to 9.8 (Opus 4.6) over 18 months at fixed 10M token budget. At 100M tokens, Opus 4.6 averaged 1.4/7 ICS steps. The study covered only 7 frontier models. Open-weight replication would extend findings. (arxiv.org/abs/2603.11214)

# Copilot vs. Autonomous: Measuring the Amplification Factor in Guided Cyber Attack Scenarios

**Problem:** MITRE OCCULT identifies the human-AI copilot paradigm as the most realistic near-term threat but the least studied. Almost all existing evaluations measure fully autonomous AI performance. We have no data quantifying how much a human operator amplifies AI performance on multi-step tasks.

**Direction:** Design a controlled study where CS students with no security background (1) attempt a 5-step CTF-style challenge alone, (2) use an LLM autonomously, and (3) use an LLM in copilot mode (human provides high-level decisions, AI executes). Measure steps completed, time, and errors in each condition. Compute a 'copilot amplification factor'.

**Why it matters:** The copilot threat model is most relevant for real attackers yet least benchmarked. Measuring amplification quantitatively would directly fill the gap identified by OCCULT and inform policy thresholds: is a novice + AI equivalent to an expert alone?

**Relevant context:** MITRE OCCULT (arxiv.org/abs/2502.15797) argues CTF-only evaluations miss copilot scenarios. HTB AI Range (Dec 2025) benchmarks AI agents and human-AI teaming side-by-side. title: CTF Difficulty Calibration Using Item Response Theory: Building a Principled Cyber Capability Scale

original_idea.body:
# CTF Difficulty Calibration Using Item Response Theory: Building a Principled Cyber Capability Scale

**Problem:** CTF benchmarks report raw solve rates (e.g., Cybench 82%) without calibrating item difficulty. A 50% solve rate on a hard challenge and a 50% rate on an easy challenge tell us different things about capability, but existing benchmarks treat them identically.

**Direction:** Apply 2-parameter IRT (difficulty + discrimination) to an existing CTF dataset (e.g., Cybench, NYU CTF Bench) using model solve/fail data across multiple models as 'examinees'. Fit IRT curves, estimate per-challenge difficulty and discrimination parameters, and generate a capability theta score for each model. Validate by checking if theta scores correlate with known model rankings.

**Why it matters:** IRT produces a principled, scale-invariant capability metric unaffected by benchmark difficulty distribution shifts, addressing the saturation problem (Cybench went 10%→82% making raw scores meaningless) and providing a foundation for longitudinal comparison.

**Relevant context:** Cambridge/Trismik applied IRT to AI evaluation (enterprise.cam.ac.uk). Cybench reached 93% saturation (CAIBench meta-benchmark, arxiv.org/html/2510.24317v1). AISI noted that no standardized longitudinal comparison methodology exists. IRT has been validated for LLM benchmarking in NLP contexts.

title: Mutation Testing for Cyber Benchmarks: Measuring Robustness of AI Performance to Challenge Perturbations

original_idea.body:
# Mutation Testing for Cyber Benchmarks: Measuring Robustness of AI Performance to Challenge Perturbations

**Problem:** AI models may be solving CTF challenges through memorization of training data rather than genuine reasoning. If a model has seen a challenge during training, solve rates are inflated. No systematic methodology exists to detect this contamination in cyber benchmarks.

**Direction:** Apply mutation testing principles from software engineering: take 10 known public CTF challenges and create 5 variants each by modifying surface features (changing IP addresses, port numbers, hash values, variable names) while preserving the underlying vulnerability class. Compare solve rates on originals vs. mutations. Large performance drops on mutations indicate memorization rather than generalization.

**Why it matters:** Benchmark contamination is a known problem in NLP benchmarks and almost certainly affects cyber benchmarks too, given models are trained on internet data including CTF writeups. Without decontamination methodology, capability measurements may be systematically inflated.

**Relevant context:** Cybench reached 82% (Irregular 2026), raising questions about whether this reflects genuine capability or memorization. CAIBench (arxiv.org/html/2510.24317v1) addressed saturation concerns. NYU CTF Bench noted challenges with reuse. Software testing mutation analysis (Gopinath et al., arxiv.org/pdf/2201.11303) provides transferable methodology.

# Longitudinal Benchmark Design: Protocol for Tracking AI Cyber Capability Over Time Without Saturation

**Problem:** Cybench went from 10% to 82% in 18 months, effectively saturating as a benchmark. No standardized methodology exists for creating benchmarks that remain valid over multi-year timescales as capabilities increase.

**Direction:** Design a benchmark construction protocol that addresses saturation: (1) tiered difficulty structure with escalating challenge classes, (2) an adaptive challenge generation pipeline that creates new challenges as existing tiers saturate, (3) an anchoring mechanism that maintains comparability across time points using IRT. Implement a small-scale version covering 3 difficulty tiers and validate that current models saturate tier 1 but not tier 3.

**Why it matters:** Without longitudinal benchmarks, the field cannot reliably track whether safety interventions are working or whether the rate of capability growth is changing. This is a foundational methodology gap identified across AISI, OCCULT, and SoK papers.

**Relevant context:** AISI noted no standardized longitudinal comparison methodology exists. Cybench 10%→82% saturation. CTFusion (OpenReview 2025) introduced streaming evaluation with live CTFs to avoid reuse. CAIBench meta-benchmark approach addresses some saturation issues but not longitudinal design.

# Prompt Injection in Tool-Augmented Offensive Agents: When the Attacker's Weapon Becomes the Backdoor

**Problem:** AI agents used for offensive red-teaming often browse adversary-controlled web pages and files as part of reconnaissance. These environments can contain prompt injections that redirect the agent. No evaluation measures how often offensive AI agents themselves become hijacked via prompt injection during an offensive engagement.

**Direction:** Set up a CTF-style target that includes prompt injection payloads embedded in web pages, file metadata, and server response headers. Run an AI agent attempting to compromise the target. Measure: (1) how often the agent successfully identifies and ignores injections, (2) how often it is redirected by them, (3) what the injections cause the agent to do (e.g., exfiltrate session tokens back to attacker's server).

**Why it matters:** If offensive AI agents are vulnerable to prompt injection from targets they attack, sophisticated defenders could use this as a counter-strategy. This also reveals a novel compounding risk: the tool meant for offense becomes an attack surface.

**Relevant context:** WASP benchmark (arxiv.org/pdf/2504.18575) measures web agent security against prompt injections. # Specialist vs. Generalist Capability Gap: A Controlled Comparison of General LLMs vs. Security-Finetuned Models

**Problem:** Security-specialized models (e.g., fine-tuned on CTF writeups, security advisories, exploit databases) may have qualitatively different capability profiles than general frontier models. The magnitude and distribution of this specialization advantage has not been systematically measured.

**Direction:** Compare 2-3 general frontier models against 2-3 security-specialized variants (e.g., models fine-tuned on security datasets available on HuggingFace) on an identical 20-challenge benchmark spanning multiple ATT&CK phases. Measure not just solve rates but failure mode patterns (wrong tool, wrong reasoning, missing knowledge). Compute a specialization delta per challenge category.

**Why it matters:** If specialization primarily helps with knowledge-based tasks (cryptography, RE) but not reasoning-based tasks (lateral movement planning), this tells us which capabilities are knowledge-limited vs. reasoning-limited — critical for understanding what training interventions change capability.

# Decompilation Capability Benchmark: Measuring AI Binary Analysis Quality Across Architecture Types

**Problem:** AISI reported sharp capability drops for reverse engineering tasks. However, no benchmark disaggregates RE capability by binary architecture (x86, ARM, MIPS, RISC-V), obfuscation level, or binary size — all of which significantly affect decompilation difficulty.

**Direction:** Create a 20-challenge decompilation benchmark with: (1) 5 clean x86 binaries, (2) 5 ARM binaries, (3) 5 lightly obfuscated x86, (4) 5 heavily obfuscated x86. For each, ask models to identify the vulnerability class (use/after/free, buffer overflow, etc.). Score accuracy against ground truth. Plot capability as a function of architecture and obfuscation level.

**Why it matters:** Embedded systems (IoT, ICS) often run ARM/MIPS architectures. If AI RE capability is weak outside x86, then IoT/ICS attack vectors remain more protected. If obfuscation reliably defeats AI analysis, this is a practical defensive recommendation.

**Relevant context:** AISI found sharp RE capability drops. VirusTotal AI pipeline (Nov 2025) achieved 0-detection malware identification. LLM4Decompile (arxiv 2505.11340) shows progress on binary decompilation. Bytebreach.com blog (2025) documented AI-assisted RE limitations on varied architectures.

title: Causal Link: Does Better Reconnaissance Cause Better Overall Attack Chain Completion?

original_idea.body:
# Causal Link: Does Better Reconnaissance Cause Better Overall Attack Chain Completion?

**Problem:** Attack chains depend on sequential steps where early failures cascade. The causal contribution of reconnaissance quality to overall chain completion has not been isolated. It is possible that AI reconnaissance is the binding constraint preventing full chain completion.

**Direction:** Design a 2-condition experiment on a 5-step attack chain: (A) AI performs end-to-end including reconnaissance, (B) human provides a perfect reconnaissance report, then AI continues from step 2. Compare completion rates. If condition B substantially outperforms A, reconnaissance is the binding constraint. Vary the quality of the human-provided recon to find the performance cliff.

**Why it matters:** If reconnaissance is the binding constraint, investments in reconnaissance tooling (web-connected agents, better scanning tools) would dramatically accelerate AI offensive capability. This is a direct threat forecasting input for defenders and evaluators.

**Relevant context:** AISI corporate range bottleneck analysis identified reconnaissance and NTLM relay as early failure points. AWS Security Agent (2025) used dedicated reconnaissance sub-agents. Context relay research (NDSS 2026) addresses context management in long attack chains. CyberExplorer found attack trajectory variance tied to discovery quality.

title: Novice vs. Expert Human Baseline: Calibrating AI Capability Against Human Skill Levels

original_idea.body:
# Novice vs. Expert Human Baseline: Calibrating AI Capability Against Human Skill Levels

**Problem:** AI capability is always reported in isolation, but the threat model requires comparison to human baselines at different skill levels (script kiddie, junior pentester, senior red teamer). No published study provides a human baseline on the same challenges used for AI evaluation.

**Direction:** Recruit 10-15 CS students with no security background and 5-10 with some CTF experience. Have each attempt a standardized 10-challenge set (same challenges run against AI). Record time-to-completion, hints used, and steps completed. Generate a 'human capability distribution'. Plot AI performance against this distribution to answer: 'at what skill percentile does AI operate?'

**Why it matters:** Saying AI completes 22/32 steps means nothing without knowing whether a median human does 5/32 or 28/32. Human baseline calibration converts raw AI scores into threat-relevant comparisons ('AI operates at the 80th percentile of professional pentesters') that policymakers and defenders can act on.

**Relevant context:** OCCULT noted CTF benchmarks lack human baselines. HTB reported AI matched 'hundreds of human teams' on easy challenges but this was not controlled. AISI estimated 22/32 steps corresponds to ~6 of the 14 hours a human expert would need — but this was expert-only estimation. SoK Potter et al. called for fine-grained risk assessment benchmarks.

# Causal Chain of ICS Attack: Mapping Which Sub-Skills Enable Each Step of a Cooling Tower Compromise

**Problem:** Models average 1.4/7 steps on the AISI ICS range. Without knowing which sub-skills (Modbus protocol knowledge, PLC programming concepts, network enumeration in OT environments) are needed for each step and which are missing, it is impossible to predict when this capability will improve.

**Direction:** Using publicly available ICS/SCADA documentation and CTF writeups from Dragos OT CTF 2025, decompose a 7-step ICS attack chain into required sub-skills per step. Test models' sub-skill knowledge via targeted Q&A (e.g., 'what Modbus function code reads coil values?'). Correlate knowledge gaps with step-level failure rates. Identify the highest-leverage missing sub-skill.

**Why it matters:** ICS attacks on critical infrastructure are the highest-consequence cyber threat. Understanding whether the 1.4/7 ceiling reflects a knowledge gap (fixable with targeted training data) or a reasoning gap (harder to address) directly informs whether ICS systems have a durable safety margin.

# Explaining the Dragos CTF vs. AISI ICS Range Discrepancy: CTF Tasks vs. Operational Tasks

**Problem:** A surprising paradox: an AI system reached Rank 1 in Dragos OT CTF 2025 (completing 32/34 challenges) while AISI frontier models average only 1.4/7 steps on an ICS cyber range. This discrepancy suggests CTF ICS challenges and operational ICS attack scenarios measure different things.

**Direction:** Categorize a sample of Dragos OT CTF challenges by type (knowledge questions, forensics puzzles, vs. operational attack simulation). Compare this distribution to AISI's ICS range step taxonomy. Hypothesize that CTF challenges over-index on knowledge and forensics while the AISI range tests operational chaining. Design 5 challenges that bridge both task types and test whether the performance gap narrows.

**Why it matters:** If CTF success grossly over-estimates real-world operational ICS attack capability, this is exactly the point MITRE OCCULT makes about CTF benchmarks generally — and it urgently applies to ICS evaluation where the stakes are critical infrastructure.

title: Replication on Cloud Infrastructure: Do Benchmark Results Transfer to AWS/GCP/Azure Attack Scenarios?

# Replication on Cloud Infrastructure: Do Benchmark Results Transfer to AWS/GCP/Azure Attack Scenarios?

**Problem:** All major published AI cyber evaluations use on-premise or simulated network environments. Real enterprise targets increasingly live in cloud environments with different attack surfaces (IAM misconfigurations, metadata service exploitation, serverless pivoting). Benchmark results may not transfer.

**Direction:** Set up a free-tier cloud environment (AWS free tier) with deliberately misconfigured IAM policies, public S3 buckets, and an exposed EC2 instance. Run AI agents on a 5-step cloud attack chain (enumeration → IAM exploitation → lateral movement → data exfiltration) and compare solve rates to equivalent on-premise network chains. Note which cloud-specific steps fail.

**Why it matters:** Over 90% of enterprise infrastructure has significant cloud footprint. Evaluations that exclude cloud attack scenarios produce capability estimates that are systematically biased away from the most relevant real-world targets.

**Relevant context:** CSA blog (Oct 2025) on AI-integrated cloud pentesting. AI-Driven Cloud Pentesting with LLMs (CSA 2025) found LLMs capable of IAM enumeration. SoK Potter et al. title: Backcast from Verifiable Safe Harbor: What Test Results Would Demonstrate AI Cannot Cross a Critical Threshold

# Backcast from Verifiable Safe Harbor: What Test Results Would Demonstrate AI Cannot Cross a Critical Threshold?

**Problem:** Current evaluations only measure what AI can do, never what it demonstrably cannot do. A safety framework requires the ability to certify that a capability threshold has NOT been crossed, not just document failures. No methodology exists for generating credible negative capability claims.

**Direction:** Define a specific capability claim: 'AI cannot complete privilege escalation from user to domain admin in an Active Directory environment without human assistance.' Design a test with statistical power analysis to reject this claim if false (N challenges, success criterion, significance threshold). Run the test and produce a confidence interval on the negative claim, not just a point estimate.

**Why it matters:** Responsible AI deployment frameworks (EU AI Act, US EO on AI) require evidence of safety, not just observed failures. A methodology for credible negative capability claims is necessary for any serious pre-deployment safety evaluation protocol.

**Relevant context:** AISI Frontier AI Trends Report addresses threshold certification. UK AISI evaluation methodology uses multi-attempt runs that provide some statistical grounding. SoK called for 'fine-grained benchmarks for risk assessment'. Statistical power analysis methods are standard in experimental psychology and medical research.
